Senses.Explanation: One’s seven-foot place on the long communal monastic platform: the allotted place where a resident hangs a bag, sits cross-legged, sleeps, eats, and conducts inquiry. Meixi Fudu answers “how does each person study non-doing?” with “straighten your back at your seven-foot place” (七尺單前豎脊梁), and elsewhere calls for crossing the legs there. Dahui Zonggao and Yuanwu Keqin likewise direct their audiences back to the place under three rafters and before the seven-foot allotment for close examination. The measured phrase therefore names the resident’s concrete place in the hall before it becomes a recurrent setting for inquiry.

Senses.Explanation: Seven hands and eight feet depicts conspicuously many-limbed, disorderly activity. Fojian Huiqin uses it in a rebuke, Zhanran Yuancheng gives it as a direct answer, and a preserved capping verse carries the same impossible-body image. The construction is evaluative and figurative in these cases; it does not assert a literal creature with seven hands and eight feet.

The monastic robe made in seven strips or panels, with the word for robe commonly left unstated. The grammar identifies the object: Yunmen Wenyan asks why one “puts on the seven-strip robe within the bell sound” (向鐘聲裏披七條), later “removes the seven-strip robe” (卸卻七條) while questioning an unnamed monk, and Wuyi Yuanlai gives the fuller “puts on the seven-strip robe” (披七條衣). Hanyue Fazang, Jifei Ruyi, and Pinjixiang Zhixiang continue Yunmen's bell-and-robe wording with the robe as the thing put on or bitten through by the sound. The words “seven strips” (七條) therefore name the counted robe, not seven unspecified items.
Senses.Note: The headword names the counted seven-strip robe even when the noun robe is omitted.

Senses.Explanation: Budai, literally 'the Cloth-Bag monk,' is the non-lineage figure defined in Chan records by the bag he carries and uses in public exchanges. His title is attested. Asked 'what is the cloth bag?' (如何是布袋), he puts the bag down; asked 'what is the matter beneath the cloth bag?' (如何是布袋下事), he shoulders it and leaves. Asked the great meaning of the buddha-teaching, he again puts it down and stands with folded hands; asked whether there is an upward matter, he shoulders it and goes. In the street he says he is waiting for a person and rejects the claimant who says he has arrived. Records raise his verse, 'Maitreya, true Maitreya, manifests countless hundreds of millions of bodies, constantly showing himself to people, while people do not recognize him' (彌勒真彌勒，分身千百億，時時示時人，時人自不識), and publicly comment on it. The Zen Budai is thus the bag-bearing street figure whose putting down, shouldering, waiting, displaying, and Maitreya verse are repeatedly raised and judged.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase “Somewhat closer” is a comparative verdict: one response is judged nearer than another without being declared complete. Somewhat closer or a little better by comparison. The phrase is attested and repeatedly serves as a qualified public appraisal. Huangbo Xiyun says that among Mazu Daoyi’s eighty-four teachers only Guizong Zhichang is somewhat closer. Xitang Zhizang summons the assembly and says that the record's unnamed participant who tries to help is somewhat closer. After an interlocutor whom the record does not name says he does not understand, Guanghui Qingshun replies that this is a little closer. Baiyan Fu says that Fu Dashi, Baozhi, and Emperor Wu still do not compare quite as well with Yan's action. Yuanwu Keqin says that being entirely unlike a list of proposed identifications is only then somewhat closer, and immediately asks why. Changqing Huileng applies the phrase after a long silence. The comparison can therefore qualify speech, silence, action, withdrawal, or the condition before a question while still withholding full approval.
